SA formulation: To properly use SA, the following formulation was used (Table 1): Table 1: Simulated annealing problem formulation for the Easom function Component Definition State (x1, x2) ∈ [−100, 100]2 Cost function f (x1, x2) (Easom function) Neighborhood Gaussian perturbation: x ′ = x + N (0, σ2), clipped to bounds Acceptance Boltzmann: ∆E < 0 ⇒ always accept; ∆E ≥ 0 ⇒ accept with P = exp(−∆E/T ) Cooling Geometric: Tk+1 = αTk; Linear: Tk+1 = Tk − γ; Logarithmic: Tk = T0 1+ln(1+k) The Boltzmann acceptance rule allows SA to escape local optima. When the temperature T is high, even large uphill moves are accepted with high probability (e.g. ∆E = 1, T = 5 ⇒ P = e −0.2 ≈ 0.82), enabling broad exploration. As T decreases, the acceptance probability drops sharply (e.g. ∆E = 1, T = 0.1 ⇒ P = e−10 ≈ 0.00005), and SA transitions into greedy exploitation. This exploration-to-exploitation shift is what makes SA effective for problems like the Easom function where the global basin is small relative to the search space. (ii) Algorithm / Pseudocode SIMULATED-ANNEALING-EASOM(x0, T0, alpha, sigma, max_iter, schedule): x <- x0; cost <- f(x); best <- (x, cost) T <- T0 for k = 1 to max_iter: x’ <- clip(x + Normal(0, sigma^2), [-100, 100]) cost’ <- f(x’) delta <- cost’ - cost if delta < 0 OR random() < exp(-delta / T): x <- x’; cost <- cost’ if cost < best.cost: best <- (x, cost) T <- cool(T, k, schedule) // geometric, linear, or logarithmic return best (iii) Experiment Plots Experiment 1 Plot is shown in Figure 1. Experiment 2 Plot is shown in Figure 2. Experiment 3 Plot is shown in Figure 3. (iv) Observations on SA Performance Experiment 1. SA performance is quite sensitive to the initial point, which makes sense given the Easom function’s needle-like structure. Runs that start closer to (π, π) or whose random walk happens to pass through the narrow global basin converge to near-optimal values (runs 3, 8, 10). In contrast, runs starting 1 Figure 1: Convergence curves for 10 different initial points. Figure 2: Convergence curves for 10 different initial temperatures. 2 Figure 3: Convergence curves for 10 different annealing schedules. far from the basin (runs 2, 6) get trapped in the flat plateau where the Easom function is essentially zero — the Gaussian perturbations produce neighbors with ∆E ≈ 0, so the Boltzmann criterion provides no gradient signal to guide the search toward (π, π). This highlights a limitation of SA: it is a memoryless method with no mechanism to systematically direct the search, unlike trajectory methods with memory such as Tabu Search. Experiment 2. There is a clear pattern tied to the Boltzmann acceptance mechanics. At T0 = 0.1, the acceptance probability for any uphill move is essentially zero (P = e−∆E/0.1 ≈ 0 for any positive ∆E), so SA degenerates into greedy hill-climbing and gets stuck immediately. At the other extreme, T0 ≥ 10,000 accepts nearly all moves — with geometric cooling at α = 0.995, the temperature after 10 000 iterations is T0 · 0.99510000. For T0 = 10,000 this is still ∼ 0.07, meaning the algorithm spends most of its budget on random exploration before ever settling. We found that moderate temperatures (T0 ∈ [1, 1000]) tend to perform best: the initial phase explores broadly enough to reach the basin near (π, π), and the cooling schedule then narrows the search to exploit that region. T0 = 1 and T0 = 50 yield the best results. Experiment 3. We observe that the cooling rate directly controls when SA transitions from exploration to exploitation. With α = 0.999 and T0 = 1000, the temperature at iteration 10 000 is 1000 · 0.99910000 ≈ 45 — still very high, so the algorithm never settles and wanders aimlessly. In contrast, α = 0.9 drops the temperature to near zero within the first ∼100 iterations, transitioning quickly to exploitation. Given that T0 = 1000 already provides substantial initial exploration, fast cooling (α = 0.9) works best here. The linear schedule with γ = 0.05 reduces T by only 0.05 per iteration, reaching T = 500 after 10 000 steps — barely any cooling at all. The logarithmic schedule (Tk = T0/(1 + ln(1 + k))) cools even more slowly: at k = 10,000, T ≈ 1000/10.2 ≈ 98. It is worth noting that the logarithmic schedule is the only one with a theoretical convergence guarantee — SA provably converges to the global optimum under logarithmic cooling via Markov chain analysis. However, this guarantee requires an impractical number of iterations (exponential in problem size), which explains why it performs poorly in practice with a fixed budget of 10 000 iterations. (v) Best Solution Table 2 shows the best solution found. We attribute this result to the geometric schedule with α = 0.995 providing a gradual transition from exploration to exploitation over 10 000 iterations. The Easom function’s difficulty comes from its needle-like structure: the function is flat (near zero) everywhere except in a tiny region around (π, π) where it plunges to −1. (vi) Code The implementation is in q1.py. 5 2 Problem 2 2.1 Deliverables (i) Problem Representation The board is a 4 × 4 grid where each cell stores (player, stone count). • Players: Black (P1 / MAX) and White (P2 / MIN). • Initial state: Black has 10 stones at (0, 0); White has 10 stones at (3, 3); all other cells empty. • Move: A player picks one of their occupied cells and a direction (8 directions: up, down, left, right, and 4 diagonals). Stones are distributed along that direction: 1 stone to the first cell, 2 to the second, and the remainder to the last reachable cell. Movement stops when hitting a wall or an opponent’s occupied cell. • Terminal condition: A player loses when they have no legal moves. Data structures class Cell: # (stones: int, player: str | None) class Move: # (player, row, col, direction) Algorithm / Pseudocode MINIMAX-ALPHA-BETA(state, player, depth, alpha, beta): if depth == 0: return (evaluate(state), None) at_max_node <- (player == MAX) best_score <- -inf if at_max_node else +inf best_move <- None for each move in legalMoves(state, player): child <- applyMove(state, move) score, _ <- MINIMAX-ALPHA-BETA(child, other(player), depth-1, alpha, beta) if (at_max_node AND score > best_score) OR (NOT at_max_node AND score < best_score): best_score <- score best_move <- move if at_max_node: alpha <- max(alpha, best_score) else: beta <- min(beta, best_score) if beta <= alpha: break // prune return (best_score, best_move) The algorithm uses a single at max node flag to unify the MAX and MIN logic: at a MAX node we initialize to −∞ and update when a child score is higher, while at a MIN node we initialize to +∞ and update when a child score is lower. Here, α represents the best (highest) value that MAX can guarantee along any path from the root — it is a lower bound that only increases. β represents the best (lowest) value MIN can guarantee — an upper bound that only decreases. Pruning fires when β ≤ α, meaning the current branch cannot improve on what is already guaranteed. This does not change the minimax value but can reduce the number of nodes explored from O(bd) to O(bd/2) in the best case with good move ordering. Hand-Worked Example We trace the full minimax tree from the initial board state using evaluate1 (−|moves(opponent)|) and depth limit d = 2 (1 ply for MAX, 1 ply for MIN). A hand-worked tree is given in Figure 4 6 Figure 4: Hand-worked demonstration of Conga solution strategy. The root is a MAX node where Black has 3 legal moves from (0, 0): diagonal (1, 1), down (1, 0), and right (0, 1). We initialize α = −∞, β = +∞. Move A (diagonal) distributes 1 stone to (1, 1) and 9 to (2, 2), and its MIN child has only 2 responses (White cannot go (−1, −1) because Black occupies (2, 2)). Both White responses — up and left — yield eval1 = −11 (White has 11 legal moves in each resulting board), so MIN returns −11 and the root updates α = max(−∞, −11) = −11. Move B (down) leads to a MIN node where the first White response evaluated is diagonal (−1, −1), which gives eval1 = −16 (White’s stones land on central positions with 16 legal moves). At this point β = min(+∞, −16) = −16, and since β = −16 ≤ α = −11 the pruning condition fires — MIN already has a value worse than what MAX is guaranteed from Move A, so the remaining 2 White responses are pruned. The same happens at Move C (right): White’s diagonal response again evaluates to −16, triggering the same β ≤ α cutoff. MAX therefore selects Move A with value −11, visiting 8 total states (1 root + 3 MIN nodes + 4 leaves). Without pruning the full tree would have 12 nodes (2 + 3 + 3 = 8 leaves), so alpha-beta eliminated 4 leaf evaluations — a 33% reduction. (ii) Random Agent and Experiment Results The random agent enumerates all legal moves for the current player and selects one uniformly at random: RANDOM-AGENT(state, player): moves <- legalMoves(state, player) return moves[random(0, |moves|-1)] Experiment results: MinMax (Black) vs Random (White). Evaluation functions considered: Table 4. Table 4: Evaluation functions used for Conga Function Formula Rationale evaluate1 −|moves(P 2)| Minimize opponent’s mobility evaluate2 |moves(P 1)| Maximize own mobility evaluate3 |moves(P 1)| − |moves(P 2)| Maximize mobility difference We chose depth d = 3 to keep response times reasonable. The branching factor in Conga can reach ∼128 (16 cells × 8 directions), so at d = 3 the worst-case tree has ∼2 million nodes before pruning. In practice, 7 alpha-beta prunes the vast majority of these. Settings: depth = 3, 5 trials per evaluation function. evaluate1: −moves(opponent) Results are shown in Table 5. Performance observations: • We found that evaluate1 (minimize opponent moves) performs best: 4/5 wins, fewest average moves (82.2), and fewest average nodes (50 361). We attribute this to the aggressive nature of directly reducing the opponent’s options — in Conga, trapping the opponent is the win condition, so an evaluation function aligned with that objective is naturally more effective. • evaluate2 (maximize own moves) is less effective with 3/5 wins. It plays defensively — keeping its own options open without actively pressuring the opponent. • evaluate3 (difference) is surprisingly the weakest (2/5 wins, most ties). We believe the combined metric dilutes the signal: the agent may sacrifice absolute pressure on the opponent to marginally improve its own mobility, leading to overly cautious play that fails to close out games. • White (Random) never wins, confirming that even a depth-3 minimax search with alpha-beta pruning dominates random play. 8 • Games that end in ties hit the 200-move limit. This is consistent with the assignment’s note that Conga (without the line-of-four win condition) is hard to finish between players of similar strength. Random Agent O(b) per move to enumerate legal moves. 10 3 Problem 3 3.1 Deliverables (i) Optimization Formulation Given n = 20 departments and n = 20 locations arranged in a 4 × 5 grid we formulate the optimization problem as: min π∈S20 n∑ i=1 n∑ j=i+1 fij · dπ(i),π(j) where π is a permutation mapping departments to locations, fij is the flow between departments i and j, and dπ(i),π(j) is the rectilinear distance between locations π(i) and π(j). (ii) Tabu Search Program Description Table 9: Tabu Search components for the QAP instance Component Description Encoding Permutation π of length 20, where π[i] = department at location i. Neighborhood All pairwise swaps of two departments: ( 20 2 ) = 190 neighbors. Move operator Swap departments at positions i and j (attribute-based tabu). Tabu list Recency-based (short-term memory): stores each swap (i, j) with a tenure counter. Moves remain tabu for tabu tenure iterations. Aspiration Override tabu if move improves best-so-far: A(s) = {s′ ∈ N (s) | E(s ′) < E(s ∗)}. Principle: “tabu prevents cycling, not progress.” Admissible set C(s) = (N (s) \ T ) ∪ A(s) — non-tabu plus aspiration-allowed moves. Stopping Fixed iteration limit (300 iterations). Next solution Best admissible neighbor: s′ = arg mins′∈C(s) E(s ′). (iii) Experiments Experiment 1 — 20 Different Initial Solutions. Settings: tabu size=15, no aspiration, no frequency. All 20 runs converge to solutions within 0.4–1.5% of optimal, demonstrating that TS is robust to the initial permutation. We observe that the best solutions (cost 1290, runs 7 and 12) are found at later iterations (228, 290), which suggests the algorithm benefits from continued intensification — the search progressively narrows into promising basins as it accumulates tabu restrictions. However, none of the 20 runs reach the optimal (1285), indicating that with a fixed tenure of 15 and no aspiration, the recency-based memory alone is not sufficient to fully explore the solution space. Experiment 2 — Different Tabu List Sizes. Settings: No aspiration, no frequency, 10 runs each. Results are shown in Table 11. Table 11: QAP results for different tabu list sizes (10 runs each) Tabu Size Avg Cost Lowest Cost Avg Error 5 1305.3 1294 20.3 10 1293.4 1285 8.4 15 1300.5 1287 15.5 20 1299.3 1287 14.3 25 1303.1 1292 18.1 We found that a tabu tenure of 10 achieves the best performance, finding the optimal solution (1285) in one run and achieving the lowest average cost (1293.4). This aligns with the lecture discussion on tabu tenure dynamics: short tenure (size 5) only prevents revisiting the last few swaps, so the search can still cycle through shallow local optima. Long tenure (sizes 20–25) overly restricts the admissible set, blocking potentially good moves and reducing the effective neighborhood. The sweet spot at ≈ n/2 = 10 provides enough memory to escape local basins without over-constraining the search. Experiment 3 — Dynamic Tabu List Size. Settings: Initial size = 15, varies by ±2 each iteration (uniformly random), 10 runs. Results are shown in Table 12. Table 12: QAP results with dynamic tabu list size (10 runs) Run Lowest Cost Found At Error 1 1287 66 2 2 1299 179 14 3 1290 155 5 4 1285 187 0 5 1292 212 7 6 1297 124 12 7 1285 169 0 8 1299 215 14 9 1287 161 2 10 1298 142 13 Summary: Avg cost = 1291.9, Lowest = 1285 (optimal), Avg error = 6.9. Dynamic sizing finds the optimal solution in 2/10 runs and achieves the lowest average error (6.9) across all experiments. We attribute this to the randomized tenure introducing beneficial diversification: when the tenure is momentarily short, the search can revisit nearby solutions to intensify around promising regions; when it spikes higher, the search is forced into unexplored territory. This approach is similar to the adaptive tenure strategy proposed by Taillard, where the tenure is periodically re-sampled from a range [Lmin, Lmax] derived from the problem size. Experiment 4 — Aspiration Criteria. Settings: tabu size=15, aspiration = best-so-far override, 10 runs. Results are shown in Table 13. Summary: Avg cost = 1296.2, Lowest = 1285 (optimal), Avg error = 11.2. 12 Table 13: QAP results with aspiration criterion (10 runs) Run Lowest Cost Found At Error 1 1297 47 12 2 1294 204 9 3 1301 53 16 4 1298 159 13 5 1287 297 2 6 1285 138 0 7 1299 104 14 8 1299 62 14 9 1308 33 23 10 1294 235 9 The aspiration criterion overrides the tabu list when a move improves on the global best: if E(s′) < E(s∗), the move is accepted even if it is tabu. This is a permission mechanism — it lifts the tabu restriction when there is clear evidence of progress. We found that aspiration allows the algorithm to reach the optimal in 1/10 runs. The average performance matches Experiment 1 (11.2 error), but the ability to seize improving moves that would otherwise be blocked adds robustness. Experiment 5 — Frequency-Based Diversification. Settings: tabu size=15, aspiration = True, fre- quency penalty = True (weight = 5), 10 runs. Results are shown in Table 14. Table 14: QAP results with frequency-based diversification (10 runs) Run Lowest Cost Found At Error 1 1301 297 16 2 1297 19 12 3 1303 235 18 4 1309 167 24 5 1298 42 13 6 1298 295 13 7 1291 248 6 8 1308 233 23 9 1300 278 15 10 1298 188 13 Summary: Avg cost = 1300.3, Lowest = 1291, Avg error = 15.3. The frequency-based penalty implements long-term memory (diversification): by adding weight × freq(i, j) to the cost of each swap, we penalize frequently used moves to push the search into unexplored regions. However, with weight = 5, this penalty is too aggressive — it distorts the actual objective value significantly, causing the algorithm to reject good moves in favor of novel but poor ones. We believe a lower weight (e.g. 1–2) or an adaptive scheme that increases the penalty only after detecting stagnation would yield better results. The key lesson is that effective diversification should complement intensification, not overpower it. The following website was used to obtain the instance: https://www.coin-or.org/SYMPHONY/branchandcut/VRP/data/A/A-n39-k6.vrp 4.1 Deliverables (i) Optimization Formulation We will be testing using A-n39-k6 consisting of 38 customers, 6 vehicles, and capacity 100. min m∑ k=1 dist(routek) subject to: (a) Each route starts and ends at the depot. (b) Each customer is visited exactly once by exactly one vehicle. (c) Total demand on each route ≤ vehicle capacity Q. where dist(routek) = d(depot, c1) + ∑|r|−1 i=1 d(ci, ci+1) + d(c|r|, depot) is the Euclidean tour distance. Solution representation. A single permutation of all 38 customers: [c1, c2, . . . , c38]. The permutation is split into routes by greedily filling each route until adding the next customer would exceed the vehicle capacity Q = 100, then starting a new route. This representation is natural for SA because perturbations (swaps, reversals, relocations) on the permutation automatically produce valid customer assignments. The route-splitting is deterministic given a permutation, similar to how the TSP is encoded as a permutation in the SA-for-TSP formulation discussed in lecture. Neighborhood operators. Three operators are selected uniformly at random each iteration: Table 17: Neighborhood operators used for SA in VRP Operator Description Swap Exchange two random customers in the permutation. 2-opt Reverse a random segment [i, j], reordering the subsequence. Or-opt Remove one customer from position i and reinsert at position j. Objective function: cost(π) = |routes|∑ k=1 dist(routek) + 1000 · max(0, |routes| − m) The penalty term discourages solutions using more than m = 6 vehicles. Distances are rounded to the nearest integer per TSPLIB EUC 2D convention. Performance Results on A-n39-k6 SA settings: T0 = 5000, α = 0.9995, max iter=200 000. The modified cost function becomes: cost(π) = |routes|∑ k=1 dist(routek) + λ1 · max(0, |routes| − m) + λ2 · ∑ k max (0, duration(routek) − Tmax) where λ1 penalizes excess vehicles (as before) and λ2 penalizes duration violations. Both penalties must be large enough that the SA search strongly prefers feasible solutions, but not so large that it cannot explore through infeasible regions during high-temperature exploration. In addition, the greedy route-splitting step must check both capacity and duration when assigning customers to a route — a customer is added to the current route only if both load + dc ≤ Q and duration + travel + servicec ≤ Tmax hold; otherwise a new route is started. This narrows the feasible region, so some capacity- feasible routes become infeasible under the duration constraint, potentially requiring more vehicles. The SA neighborhood operators themselves remain unchanged. Legal moves: 9 Legal moves: 8 Is terminal: False (ii) Part B: Depth-Limited Minimax A pseudocode implementation is given below. MINIMAX(state, depth, maximizing): nodes_expanded += 1 if isTerminal(state): return utility(state), None if depth == 0: return evaluate(state), None moves <- legalMoves(state) if maximizing: best_val <- -inf; best_move <- None for each move in moves: child <- applyMove(state, move, ’X’) val, _ <- MINIMAX(child, depth-1, False) if val > best_val: best_val <- val; best_move <- move return (best_val, best_move) else: best_val <- +inf; best_move <- None for each move in moves: child <- applyMove(state, move, ’O’) val, _ <- MINIMAX(child, depth-1, True) if val < best_val: best_val <- val; best_move <- move return (best_val, best_move) Evaluation function (at depth cutoff): ˆE(s) = open lines(X) − open lines(O) 18 where an open line for player P is any row, column, or diagonal containing no opponent marks. There are 8 possible lines to check (3 rows + 3 columns + 2 diagonals). This is the same heuristic e(p) = #open(X) − #open(O) discussed in lecture for tic-tac-toe evaluation. (iii) Part C: Alpha-Beta Pruning A pseudocode implementation is given below. ALPHA-BETA(state, depth, alpha, beta, maximizing): nodes_expanded += 1 if isTerminal(state): return utility(state), None if depth == 0: return evaluate(state), None moves <- legalMoves(state) if maximizing: best_val <- -inf; best_move <- None for each move in moves: child <- applyMove(state, move, ’X’) val, _ <- ALPHA-BETA(child, depth-1, alpha, beta, False) if val > best_val: best_val <- val; best_move <- move alpha <- max(alpha, best_val) if beta <= alpha: break // prune return (best_val, best_move) else: best_val <- +inf; best_move <- None for each move in moves: child <- applyMove(state, move, ’O’) val, _ <- ALPHA-BETA(child, depth-1, alpha, beta, True) if val < best_val: best_val <- val; best_move <- move beta <- min(beta, best_val) if beta <= alpha: break // prune return (best_val, best_move) (iv) Part D: Experimental Comparison From the empty initial board (X to move): Table 22 compares Minimax and Alpha-Beta at different depths.
